source.title: Lorentz Framework for Semantic Segmentation
source.authors: Zahid Hasan; Masud Ahmed; Nirmalya Roy

record.tranche_reason: The study compares loss-surface flatness in Lorentz and Euclidean segmentation models, but does not measure whether sharpness tracks the training–test gap.
record.gate_note: The paper reports segmentation and zero-shot results, but these do not test the listed same-distribution generalization versions. Its loss-surface comparison is the only result related to V7; it does not measure a training–test gap or magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any listed version. Section 5.4 compares qualitative loss-surface flatness, but does not measure its association with training–test gaps, establish similarly low training losses, or compare gap-ranking measures as V7 requires. Segmentation performance and zero-shot retrieval do not test the other versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes Section 5.4: the authors report flatter Lorentz minima, invoke a flatness–generalization link to explain performance, and leave the mechanism for future work. Their broader conclusion also emphasizes hierarchical consistency, zero-shot generalization, uncertainty estimation, and efficient low-dimensional representations; the flatness comparison does not establish V7.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares loss landscapes of Lorentz and Euclidean segmentation models; it does not use the magnitude-aware sharpness and generalization-gap comparison specified in V7.
record.method_sensitivity: The loss-surface examples use DeepLabV3 on Cityscapes and SegFormer on COCO-Stuff.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 5.4 and Figure 16 qualitatively describe flatter loss surfaces for Lorentz models than Euclidean counterparts using two random perturbation directions with filter normalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lorentz segmentation models exhibit qualitatively flatter loss surfaces than Euclidean counterparts in the reported DeepLabV3–Cityscapes and SegFormer–COCO-Stuff comparisons.

record.problems: The flatness comparison is qualitative and shown for two examples; no training–test gap or magnitude-aware sharpness statistic is reported.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported outcomes directly test the listed versions; benchmark segmentation, cross-dataset and zero-shot results are outside their scope.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out accuracy under the same architectures and training recipes.
Test error as network width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under specified tuning conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove the penalty.
Dropout effects on held-out error across training-set sizes and augmentation conditions.
Association between magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance and training–test gaps among similarly fitted networks; ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Change V7 from tested_not_extracted to not_tested. R1's qualitative finding can remain as an out-of-version result. E1 is supported by the supplied Figure 16 caption despite the record's failed text-match verification.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test performance.
Width sweep past interpolation and test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets.
The paper compares loss-surface flatness but does not measure magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance against the training–test gap or compare measures by gap-ranking ability.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.subject: Lorentz model and its Euclidean counterpart (model names not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Perturbed model weights along two random directions to visualize loss surfaces; compared Lorentz and Euclidean models.
rows.value: The Lorentz model is described as converging to flatter minima than its Euclidean counterpart.
rows.note: The paper links flat minima to improved generalization but reports no training–test gap, magnitude-aware sharpness measure, or quantitative comparison.
rows.check: The qualitative flatness finding is accurately reported, but cannot establish V7's sharpness–generalization-gap relationship. Filter normalization is stated; no quantitative perturbation-tolerance statistic or training–test gap is reported. The subjects are identified as DeepLabV3 on Cityscapes and SegFormer on COCO-Stuff, so 'model names not stated' is incorrect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
